title: Measuring the curvature of an ion beam
stem:
A narrow beam of positive ions enters a uniform magnetic field at right angles. Its speed is fixed at $4.00 \times 10^5$ m s⁻¹. A camera records the radius of the circular arc. Assume the field and speed uncertainties are negligible. Each radius has an uncertainty of ±0.2 cm. The readings are simulated.

| Magnetic field / mT | 20.0 | 25.0 | 40.0 | 50.0 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Radius / cm | 10.0 | 8.1 | 5.0 | 4.1 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the 25.0 mT reading to calculate the magnitude of the charge-to-mass ratio of an ion.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the first and last readings and their uncertainties to assess the prediction that radius is inversely proportional to field strength.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The beam initially travels to the right and bends upwards on the camera image. Determine the direction of the field relative to the image. Explain why the speed is constant along the arc.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: At larger fields the arcs are smaller. Suggest one change to the imaging procedure that would reduce the fractional uncertainty in their radii.

steps.text: Equate the magnitudes $qvB=mv^2/r$ and rearrange to $q/m=v/(Br)$.
Convert the radius to 0.081 m and the field to 0.0250 T.
$1.98 \times 10^8$ C kg⁻¹.
Compare $Br$ at both extremes using consistent units, for example mT cm.
The intervals are 196–204 and 195–215 mT cm. They overlap.
The measurements are consistent with a constant product within uncertainty. Two readings do not establish a unique law.
Into the page, by the right-hand rule for positive charge.
The magnetic force is perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity.
It does no work, so the kinetic energy and speed stay constant.
For example, increase the calibrated image magnification while keeping the arc in view.
The same physical arc spans more pixels, reducing the fractional effect of locating its edge. Credit a circle fit using many calibrated positions with an appropriate explanation.

title: Finding a camera offset by reversing a field
stem:
A positive-ion beam travels horizontally at $2.00 \times 10^5$ m s⁻¹ between parallel plates of length 0.0800 m and separation 0.0200 m. Ignore gravity and fringing. With the plate voltage reversed the electric field reverses. The signed camera reading at the plate exit includes an unknown constant offset. Positive displacement is upwards. Each reading has uncertainty ±0.10 mm. The data are simulated.

| Potential difference / V | −40 | −20 | +20 | +40 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Camera reading / mm | −4.30 | −1.90 | +2.90 | +5.30 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the two 40 V readings to determine the camera offset and the magnitude of the beam displacement caused by a 40 V potential difference.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the charge-to-mass ratio of the ions using the corrected displacement.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Use the two 20 V readings to test a prediction of the uniform-field model.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Estimate the maximum absolute uncertainty in the corrected 4.80 mm displacement from the two readings. Explain whether taking many pairs would eliminate an error in the stated plate separation.

steps.text: The offset has the same sign in both readings while the physical displacement changes sign.
Offset is the mean, +0.50 mm.
Field displacement is half the difference, 4.80 mm.
Transit time is $0.0800/(2.00 \times 10^5)=4.00 \times 10^{-7}$ s.
Use $y=at^2/2$ to obtain $a=6.00 \times 10^{10}$ m s⁻².
$3.00 \times 10^7$ C kg⁻¹.
The half-difference at 20 V is 2.40 mm.
At fixed speed and geometry the deflection should be proportional to voltage. Doubling 20 V gives twice the displacement, as observed.
For a half-difference, add the two absolute limits and divide by two.
Maximum uncertainty is 0.10 mm.
Repeats may reduce random scatter but leave a common error in plate separation and therefore in the inferred field.

title: A crossed-field selector with a residual field
stem:
Positive ions pass through perpendicular electric and magnetic fields at right angles to their velocity. For each applied coil setting a student adjusts an opposing electric field until the beam shows no deflection. The applied magnetic field is accurate. A small, constant background magnetic field may also act along the coil axis. Electric-field readings have uncertainty ±0.10 kV m⁻¹. The readings are simulated.

| Applied magnetic field / mT | 4.0 | 6.0 | 8.0 | 10.0 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Balancing electric field / kV m⁻¹ | 2.40 | 3.40 | 4.40 | 5.40 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the end readings, determine the gradient of balancing electric field against applied magnetic field in SI units and interpret it physically.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Estimate the background field, including its direction relative to the applied field.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A second student says the non-zero intercept proves that there is a background magnetic field. Evaluate this claim and suggest a measurement that would distinguish a background field from an offset in the electric-field reading.

steps.text: $5.0 \times 10^5$ m s⁻¹.
Zero deflection requires $qE=qvB_{total}$, so the gradient is the selected speed.
The electric-field intercept is $2400-(5.0 \times 10^5)(0.004)=400$ V m⁻¹.
Divide the intercept by the selected speed.
$8.0 \times 10^{-4}$ T or 0.80 mT, in the same direction as the applied field.
A constant electric-field zero error also shifts the intercept, so this dataset alone cannot distinguish the explanations.
Measure the actual magnetic field with a separately zeroed probe when the coil current is zero (or independently calibrate the electric-field reading).
A field of about 0.80 mT at zero current supports the magnetic explanation; a zero field directs attention to the electric-field offset.
